Adaptive TSCH Scheduling for Emergency Packets
in High-Density Low-Power and Lossy Networks

Jianan Zhang, Jiamei Lv, Member, IEEE, Hailang Zhang, Yi Gao, Member, IEEE, Wei Dong, Member, IEEE,

Abstract—High-density low-power and lossy networks (LLNs)
for IoT applications (e.g., smart cities) urgently require low
latency in emergencies like fires. However, existing hash-based or
traffic-aware Time Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) scheduling
methods fall short in such emergency scenarios. These methods
lack both dedicated scheduling mechanisms for emergency packets and effective conflict resolution strategies, thereby resulting
in frequent collisions and urgent traffic latency that fails to
meet response demands. While reinforcement learning (RL)-
based schemes can mitigate these issues through multi-objective
optimization, their high computational and energy overheads
place stringent demands on the capabilities of edge nodes. To
address these challenges, We propose ATSE, an adaptive TSCH
scheduling for emergency packets in high-density LLNs. TSE
employs subtree-segregated time-slot allocation to assign regular
and emergency packets to independent subtree resources for
precise scheduling, combined with temporal emergency timeslot adjustment to dynamically reallocate slots for non-real-time
emergency packets, ensuring low-latency delivery. For conflict
avoidance, we design an Nhash-based conflict avoidance method
via selective time-slot segment partitioning, allowing conflicting
packets to request resources from sinks in dedicated segments,
thereby reducing collisions and control overhead. Additionally,
ATSE integrates multi-sink load balancing to evenly distribute
dynamic network traffic, improving overall transmission performance and resource utilization. We implement ATSE on Contiki
OS and evaluate it in large-scale, high-density scenarios. Experimental results show that ATSE outperforms baseline methods,
reducing latency by 18.6%, improving reliability by 10.5%, and
lowering energy consumption by 10.6%.

Index Terms—High-density LLNs, TSCH scheduling, emer-

gency packets, conflict avoidance, load balance.

However, this deterministic periodic scheduling mechanism
also imposes a structural constraint on the scheduled transmission latency of packets.In TSCH schedule, all transmissions
are restricted by the preconfigured slotframe, and a node can
transmit only when its scheduled transmission slot arrives,
rather than immediately after packet generation. In highdensity deployments, a large number of nodes share limited
slot resources. When emergency traffic occurs, packets often
have to wait for several individual slots or even a full slotframe
before they can be transmitted. Consequently, TSCH struggles
to meet the real-time requirements of emergency services (e.g.,
fire alarm systems) [6].

Several TSCH scheduling mechanisms [7]–[12] have been
proposed to improve network performance. One category
focuses on hash-based autonomous scheduling approaches,
such as Orchestra [10] and ALICE [7], which compute transmission slots using deterministic hash functions based on node
identifiers, link information, or routing states. These schemes
enable fully distributed operation without explicit negotiation
overhead and offer high scalability. However, multiple nodes
may hash to the same slot in dense deployments, leading
to increased collisions and prolonged delays, particularly
for latency-sensitive emergency packets. Another category
includes traffic-aware or dynamic scheduling methods, such as
OST [8], MSF [11], and LDSF [12]. These approaches adjust
slot assignments according to queue occupancy, traffic load,
or network topology dynamics. For example, OST extends
autonomous scheduling by activating additional cells based
on traffic demand, while LDSF partitions slotframes into
blocks and assigns them according to hop distance. Although
these mechanisms can reduce end-to-end delay and improve
reliability under varying traffic conditions, they generally lack
explicit prioritization mechanisms for emergency traffic and
do not effectively address slot conflicts in large-scale highdensity networks. The third category leverages reinforcement
learning (RL) to optimize slot allocation. Methods such as
HRL-TSCH [9] employ learning agents to adaptively schedule
transmissions in response to traffic conditions. Although RLbased approaches can improve responsiveness for emergency
packets, their computational and energy overhead is too high
for resource-constrained LLN nodes, limiting practical deployment.

In summary, existing TSCH scheduling schemes either
cannot ensure timely delivery of emergency traffic, suffer from
slot conflicts in dense deployments, or introduce excessive
overhead. Therefore, a lightweight adaptive mechanism that
provides both emergency prioritization and conflict avoidance
is required. To achieve these goals, there are two key chal-

 lenges as follows:

How to allocate time-slot resources between emergency
and regular data packets in high-density networks? In highdensity LLNs, a large number of sensor nodes continuously
generate periodic data (e.g., heartbeat and monitoring messages), occupying most available time-slot resources. Existing
dynamic allocation methods cannot provide timely access for
emergency packets Orchestra [10] computes transmission slots
using hash-based offsets, where the randomness of hashing
may postpone the assigned slot of an emergency packet,
leading to long waiting delays. OST [8] adopts the binary
resource tree (m,n) allocation strategy and adjusts scheduling
according to traffic load. However, regular traffic typically
occupies most slots,
leaving only sparsely distributed idle
slots with large intervals. Consequently, emergency packets
cannot promptly obtain nearby transmission opportunities. As
illustrated in Fig. 1, neither method completes emergency
transmission within two slots, and the latency increases by
50% and 300%, respectively. Therefore, designing a time-slot
allocation mechanism that preserves resource efficiency while
ensuring real-time delivery of emergency packets remains a
critical challenge.

How to achieve conflict avoidance for concurrent transmission of multi-source packets via lightweight mechanisms?
In high-density networks, simultaneous transmissions from
multiple nodes intensify competition for limited time-slot
resources [13], thereby significantly increasing the probability
of packet collisions. When multiple emergency packets are
scheduled within the same time slot, concurrent transmissions
lead to signal superposition and mutual interference at the
receiver, preventing correct packet decoding. This results in
transmission failures, retransmissions, and consequently increased latency. Existing approaches mitigate such conflicts
through inter-node negotiation mechanisms (e.g., RTS/CTSlike signaling) [14], where control packets are exchanged to
coordinate channel access. Although effective in reducing collision probability, the additional control signaling incurs nonnegligible communication and energy overhead. Therefore,
achieving efficient conflict avoidance while maintaining low
overhead remains a critical technical challenge.

To tackle these key challenges, we propose ATSE, an
adaptive TSCH scheduling mechanism for emergency packets
in high-density LLNs. First, to achieve precise slot allocation,
ATSE introduces a subtree-segregated time-slot allocation. In
the binary resource tree, left-subtree slots are preferentially
assigned to regular traffic, while emergency packets are allocated right-subtree resources, enabling prioritized and timely
transmission through fragmented slot resources. For emergency packets that cannot satisfy latency constraints under the
initial allocation, ATSE further employs temporal emergency
time-slot adjustment mechanism to dynamically reallocates
slots, ensuring deadline compliance. Second, ATSE adopts
an Nhash-based conflict avoidance method for lightweight
conflict avoidance. Each slot is divided into multiple segments,
and a hash function based on the node ID and subnetwork
ID determines the control signaling segment. To reduce overhead, segmentation is performed only once across consecutive slots, avoiding repeated partitioning operations. This

design eliminates explicit negotiation and effectively reduces
control collisions and associated communication and energy
costs. Third, ATSE incorporates a multi-sink load balancing
mechanism to dynamically distribute traffic among sinks in
large-scale and dense deployments, thereby improving overall
network performance and resource utilization. We implement
ATSE on Contiki OS [15] and conduct extensive evaluations
using the Cooja simulator [16] under large-scale network
settings. Experiments demonstrate that ATSE outperforms
baseline approaches by reducing latency by 18.6%, improving
reliability by 10.6%, and lowering energy consumption by
10.5%, highlighting its effectiveness and scalability.

Contributions: Our main contributions in this paper are

summarized as follows:

• We propose ATSE, an adaptive TSCH scheduling mechanism for emergency packets in high-density LLNs. ATSE
integrates a subtree-segregated slot allocation method
with a temporal emergency slot adjustment mechanism
to guarantee low-latency delivery, and incorporates an
Nhash-based lightweight conflict avoidance design that
eliminates explicit negotiation while efficiently resolving
multi-source transmission conflicts.

• To enhance overall

transmission performance and resource utilization, we design a multi-sink load balance
method to balance sink loads in dynamic networks.
• We implement ATSE on Contiki OS and perform comprehensive large-scale evaluations in Cooja, validating
its practicality, scalability, and performance gains across
diverse traffic and network scenarios.

II. BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION

A. Preliminary of IEEE 802.15.4e TSCH

TSCH is a key communication advancement for Low-Power
and Lossy Networks and industrial Internet of Things (IIoT)
applications [17]. It is integrated into the IEEE 802.15.4e standard [18], which is an extension of the IEEE 802.15.4 standard
for LR-WPAN. TSCH partitions the available frequency band
into time-slots, with each device operating per a specific timeslot schedule that dictates data transmission/reception timing
and enables coordinated communication among network devices. TSCH also introduces the slotframe, a two-dimensional
time-frequency scheduling table defining the structure and
organization of time-slots in wireless networks. The slotframe
is updated periodically. To transmit queued packets, nodes
first request time-slot resources from the sink node, which
allocates a unique time-slot resource to each node based on
node-specific information (e.g., node ID). Nodes then transmit
data via the allocated time-slot resources, and this schedule
remains unchanged for the entire cycle.

B. The Failure of Existing Works in Emergency Scenarios

Numerous prior works [7], [8], [10] have explored key
aspects of TSCH time-slot scheduling, including traffic-aware
resource allocation and autonomous scheduling mechanism
design. Orchestra [10] and OST [8] stand out as the most
representative schemes. Orchestra is an autonomous TSCH


Fig. 1. The scheduling example with Orchestra, OST and our idea. Orchestra
and OST increase the latency of emergency packet 50% and 300% respectively. Our idea can meet the low-latency requirement of emergency packet.

scheduling scheme for RPL networks [19], which computes
each node’s schedule table via a predefined hash function and
the node’s address information, preserving TSCH’s inherent
robustness under nondeterministic conditions. OST dynamically adjusts time-slot allocation according to real-time traffic,
boosting network reliability and energy efficiency. Each node
calculates required slots based on local traffic and network
topology. Tree nodes (represented by tuple (m, n), where m
specifies TSCH slotframe length 2m and n defines slot offset)
enable inter-node allocation. Nodes request additional slots
from intended receivers, which allocate available resources
from their own trees, realizing dynamic scheduling to enhance
network reliability and energy efficiency.

While Orchestra provides an effective autonomous scheduling solution and OST adapts well to traffic fluctuations and
topology changes, both fail to meet real-time demands in
emergency scenarios. We illustrate this using a fire alert
scenario where gateway A connects via single-hop to smoke
detectors C/D, temperature sensor B, and humidity sensor E.
In slotframe 1, B and E are assigned 2 and 1 slots for sensor
data, while C and D each get 1 slot for heartbeat packets. Node
C sends emergency packets at slot 1, and C/D simultaneously
transmit emergency packets at slot 8, as shown in Fig. 1 (blue:
pre-allocated slots, green: newly allocated slots for emergency
packets).

The key limitation is prolonged idle-slot waiting: Orchestra
fixes transmission slots via hash, so detector D (offset 2)
conflicts when sending emergency data, resulting in latency
equal to the full slotframe. OST’s binary resource tree allows
D to transmit no earlier than offset 5, causing 3-slot latency.
For events requiring transmission within 2 slots, OST and
Orchestra incur 50% and 300% higher latency, failing to meet
low-latency emergency requirements.

C. Motivation

Existing methods [20] suffer from densely packed timeslots—for example, slots 0–4 in Fig. 1 are fully occupied
by regular traffic, leaving no idle slots for burst emergency
transmissions. To address this, we propose interleaved allocation within the binary resource tree. Regular packets are first
assigned to the left-subtree, then gradually to the right-subtree,
leaving gaps for urgent transmissions, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

III. ATSE OVERVIEW AND DESIGN

A. Overview

Fig. 2 illustrates the architecture of ATSE, which comprises
three core modules: emergency-aware time-slot scheduling
(Section III-B), Nhash-based conflict avoidance(Section III-C)
and multi-sink load balance (Section III-D). When a node
joins the network, it first selects a low-load sink through the
multi-sink load balancing module to prevent uneven resource
distribution and ensure efficient utilization of time-slot resources. At the beginning of each cycle, the sink generates
a binary resource tree and performs initial time-slot allocation
for regular packets from connected nodes. Regular packets are
assigned to left-subtree slots first, with the right subtree gradually activated as needed, while reserving slots for emergency
packets. For dynamically arriving emergency packets that cannot meet low-latency requirements through regular allocation,
the temporal emergency time-slot adjustment mechanism is
triggered, prioritizing the node’s own slots and borrowing
free slots from high-load nodes when necessary to satisfy
strict response deadlines. The Nhash-based conflict avoidance
mechanism provides a lightweight negotiation framework to
resolve concurrent access conflicts among multi-source emergency packets, reducing overall energy consumption.

B. Emergency-aware Time-slot Scheduling

The core principle of this allocation strategy lies in prioritizing left-subtree slot resources for regular packets, whereas
emergency packets are allocated to free slots in the rightsubtree. Specifically, during the regular slot allocation phase,
the sink node prioritizes occupying free slots in the leftsubtree. It gradually activates the right-subtree when the
left-subtree approaches saturation, and always follows the
left-first-then-right allocation rule. This sequential allocation
method naturally forms slot resource gaps in the right-subtree
and emergency packets can complete timely transmission by
leveraging these gaps, thereby reducing delays caused by slot
waiting.

2) Temporal emergency time-slot adjustment: Although
fragment gaps in the right subtree provide partial support
for emergency packet transmission, such passive availability
cannot guarantee low-latency delivery under extreme network
load, where both subtrees of the binary resource tree are nearly
fully occupied. As illustrated in Fig. 3, an emergency packet
arriving at slot 1 may only access slot 7, which is the sole
remaining free slot, resulting in a delay of up to six slots. Such
waiting latency violates the emergency response constraint.

To address this limitation, we introduce a time-bounded
emergency slot adjustment strategy that actively reallocates

Fig. 3. The example of the scheduling under extremely high load network

limited slot resources to satisfy strict response deadlines. We
assume that each emergency event must be responded to within
K slots. Accordingly, an emergency packet arriving at slot T
must be transmitted no later than T +K. The proposed strategy
follows a priority-based and minimal-disturbance principle.
First, the emergency-sending node attempts to reuse its own
regular transmission slots within the response window [T ,
T + K − 1], which avoids inter-node coordination and reduces
control overhead. If local resources are insufficient, the node
selectively reassigns regular slots from the node with the
highest regular traffic volume within the response window,
concentrating adjustments where slot density is greatest and
limiting global scheduling disruption. To further minimize
overhead, displaced regular packets are not immediately renegotiated but are compensated during the negotiation phase of
the subsequent slotframe.

With this adjustment strategy, emergency packets can meet
strict latency requirements even in slot-scarce scenarios. Additionally, prioritizing the reuse of local slots significantly
reduces inter-node communication overhead associated with
dynamic slot reassignment.

C. Nhash-based Conflict Avoidance

In high-density scenarios,

increased node load elevates
emergency packet conflict probability [21]. When conflicts
occur, nodes compete for the same slot due to bypassing
negotiation, lacking control information exchange and sink
node scheduling. Inspired by the CTS/RTS mechanism [14],
we propose an Nhash-based conflict avoidance method for
emergency packets without negotiation. TSCH slots are divided into five sub-segments:
three for emergency packet
application, one for the sink node to broadcast slot scheduling
info, and one reserved for emergency data transmission.

The application segments’ offsets are determined by the

NHash is designed to map input values to pseudo-random
but deterministic positions within a slot, using bitwise shifts,
XOR, and the constant C to ensure sufficient diffusion and
reduce collisions. Specifically, we set C = 0x9e3779b9 and
M = 256, where M defines the hash range. The segment offset
is then calculated via Eq.2, where ID, N ID and LSG denote
node ID, network ID and number of segments respectively.
The ID is shifted 16 bits and combined with N ID as the input
to NHash, generating a unique hash value. Taking modulo LSG
maps the hash to a slot segment, providing each node with a
deterministic yet pseudo-random segment assignment, thereby
reducing collisions without explicit coordination.

This dynamic offset calculation mechanism effectively
synchronizes transmission requests and substantially lowers
packet collision risks. Upon determining the offset of their
assigned segments, each end node sends a control packet to the
sink node to request permission for emergency packet transmission in the current slot. The sink node performs allocation
per the slot allocation and adjustment method, then broadcasts
the final emergency slot allocation result to all end nodes via
the slot’s dedicated segment. Subsequently, end nodes assigned
slots transmit emergency packets through the remaining segments. This strategic use of time resources ensures orderly,
standardized communication even during emergencies.

Moreover, to reduce sub-segment division-induced overhead
and transmission performance loss, we optimize the slot selection strategy to ensure at least one sub-segmented slot in
any M consecutive slots, avoiding packet conflicts and cutting
down network performance loss and extra overhead.

D. Multi-Sink Load Balance

To further optimize the performance of the proposed method
in large-scale high-density network scenarios, we propose a
load balance strategy for multi-sink networks. This strategy
aims to achieve balanced resource utilization among the subnetworks corresponding to each sink node, thereby improve
the overall network performance. Traditional slot allocation
evaluation typically characterizes the slot resource utilization
state of a sink node by its overall slot utilization rate. However,
in the allocation method we proposed, emergency data packets
need to be incorporated as a consideration factor. For this
reason, this paper proposes a slot utilization scoring index
(Score) based on the slot utilization rates of the left and right
subtrees to evaluate the slot resource utilization efficiency of
each sink node, with its calculation formula given in Eq. 3.

Score(n) = kPregular + (1 − k)Pemergency

(3)

where Pregular is the proportion of slots occupied by regular
packets in the left-subtree of sink node n, and Pemergency
is the proportion of slots occupied by emergency packets
in the right-subtree of sink node n. The parameter kis the
weight for the proportion of slots occupied by regular packets
in the left-subtree of sink node n. In our strategy, a lower
score indicates abundant slot resources of the node, suitable
for new node access. Moreover, when a new node joins the
network, it selects the subnet with the lowest score based on
the total score of each subnet in the received EB packets.
The synchronization mechanism of TSCH sends EB control
packets for time synchronization, and nodes use this information to join the network. The multi-sink load balance strategy
maximizes the balance of slot resource utilization efficiency
of sink nodes across subnets, avoiding increased emergency
packet transmission delay caused by excessively high node
load, and thus improving overall network performance.

E. Complexity Analysis

In this subsection, we analyze the computational complexity of ATSE, which mainly arises from two processes: the
allocation of regular traffic slots and the scheduling of emergency packets. For regular traffic, the subtree-segregated slot
allocation requires traversing the resource tree and updating
the allocation state for each of the N end nodes, leading
to a complexity on the order of O(N log N ). For emergency
packets, each of the M packets must be scheduled within its
predefined response window of K slots. In the worst case,
a packet may need to check all K slots to find a suitable
transmission opportunity, resulting in a worst-case complexity
of O(K · M ). Therefore, the overall worst-case complexity
of ATSE can be expressed as O(N log N + K · M ). In
practice, the response window K is typically small and the
number of emergency packets M is much smaller than the
number of end nodes (M << N ), which limits the additional
overhead introduced by emergency scheduling. As a result,
the overall complexity remains dominated by the O(N log N )
term, allowing ATSE to maintain efficient operation even as
the network scale increases.

Moreover, several design choices enhance ATSE’s scalability. Slot allocation is centrally managed by sink nodes,
eliminating costly global coordination among end nodes.
Meanwhile, the NHash-based conflict avoidance mechanism
maps multi-source packets to deterministic pseudo-random
slot segments without explicit negotiation. This lightweight
design keeps communication overhead low, allowing ATSE
to scale efficiently while maintaining reliable and low-latency
performance in dense and dynamic networks.

IV. EVALUATION

A. Experiment Setup

1) Experiment environments and Baselines: We implement
ATSE on ContikiOS [15], evaluate and compare it against
ALICE [7], OST [8], SmarTiSCH [22], and LDSF [12] across
various metrics and scenarios using the Cooja simulator [16].
Experiments are conducted in this simulator with a large-scale
TSCH network consisting of 3 sink nodes and 75 end nodes,
where each end node connects to its sink via a single hop.

2) Metrics: we select the latency of emergency data packets, the packet delivery ratio of nodes (PDR), and the radio
duty cycle of nodes as the evaluation metrics for the experiment.

3) Setup: The experiments are run for 200 cycles each
time. To adjust the network traffic load, the number of regular
packets transmitted by each node per cycle is configured. For

B. Overall Performance

1) Different traffic load: We first evaluated performance
under varying traffic loads using a mesh network with 75
end nodes and 3 sink nodes, where each end node connects
via a single hop to its sink and 10 emergency packets are
generated per cycle. The traffic load is varied from 20 to
to 64
120 packets per cycle. The slotframe length is set
(i.e., 26), with each timeslot lasting 20 ms. As shown in
Fig. 5, ATSE consistently outperforms baseline methods in
emergency packet latency, PDR, and radio duty cycle under
both low and high traffic loads. Fig. 5(a) shows that ATSE
reduces emergency packet latency by 13.7%∼59.6% under
low traffic and 20.8%∼53.4% under high traffic compared
with baselines. This improvement stems from the subtreesegregated time-slot allocation and temporal slot adjustment
mechanisms, which exploit idle right-subtree slot fragments to
promptly schedule emergency packets, while existing methods
must wait for later idle slots. Fig. 5(b) shows that ATSE
maintains a PDR above 95%, outperforming other methods by
8.1%∼19.3% as traffic increases, due to its conflict avoidance
mechanism. Fig. 5(c) further shows that ATSE reduces radio
duty cycle by 15.3%∼24.3% under high traffic load, since its
lightweight conflict avoidance avoids costly node negotiations,
whereas other methods incur frequent retransmissions and
longer active periods.

2) Different quantities of emergency data packets: Subsequently, we evaluated network performance under varying
numbers of emergency packets. The experiments used the
same network topology (with 3 sink nodes and 75 end

nodes), with the traffic load of 60 packets per cycle, while
the number of emergency packets was gradually increased
from 10 to 40 per cycle. The slotframe length is set
32 (i.e., 25), with each timeslot having a duration of 20ms.
Fig. 6 shows the results: as the number of emergency packets
increases, ATSE consistently outperforms baseline schemes,
achieving an average latency reduction of 14.6%∼54.7%, a
PDR improvement of 3.7%∼39.6%, and a radio duty cycle
reduction of 7.7%∼21.8%. This performance gain stems from
ATSE’s subtree-segregated slot allocation, which leverages
idle right-subtree slots for timely emergency packet transmission, and its Nhash-based conflict avoidance combined
with temporal slot adjustment, ensuring that packets failing to
acquire resources are rescheduled promptly. When emergency
packet load reaches 40 per cycle, ATSE reduces latency and
radio duty cycle over 18.6% and 10.6%, respectively, while
improving PDR over 10.5% compared with other methods.

C. Scalability Evaluation

1) Performance under different network scale: We further
evaluated ATSE’s scalability with varying network topologies:
end nodes ranging from 30 to 90 and sink nodes from 3
to 5. The experiments are configured with a traffic load of
60 packets per cycle, including 20 emergency packets. The
slotframe length is also set to 32. Fig. 7(a–c) shows that
increasing the number of sink nodes enlarges the allocable
idle time-slot resources. More sinks allow traffic to be distributed across multiple collection points, reducing congestion at individual sinks. Leveraging the load-balancing strategy and subtree-segregated time-slot allocation, ATSE evenly
distributes regular packets while reserving sufficient rightsubtree resources for emergency transmissions. This enables
emergency packets to access available slots quickly, resulting in 12.3%∼53.6% latency reduction, 4.3%∼9.5% PDR

V. RELATED WORK

Numerous studies have investigated TSCH scheduling
mechanisms [29], which can be broadly categorized into hashbased methods, traffic-aware methods, and RL-based methods,
as summarized in Table II.

Hash-based methods. Hash-based TSCH scheduling computes transmission slots deterministically without negotiation.
Methods like Orchestra [10] and ALICE [7] assign slots using
node IDs or routing information for lightweight distributed
operation. However, deterministic slot mapping increases slot
overlap in dense networks, leading to more collisions and delay, especially harmful for latency-sensitive emergency packets.

Traffic-aware methods.Traffic-aware TSCH scheduling adjusts cell allocation based on load or queue status. MSF [11]
dynamically negotiates cells via queue thresholds, OST [8]
activates extra cells under high traffic, and LDSF [24] divides
slotframes into hop-based blocks to reduce interference and
delay. TESLA [12] adaptively adjusts the slotframe length
according to traffic dynamics, enabling elastic resource provisioning to improve latency and reliability under varying
load conditions. While these schemes enhance adaptability
and reliability, they rely on reactive load estimation and lack
prioritization for emergency packets. Frequent negotiation also
adds overhead in large-scale dense networks.

RL-based methods. RL-based TSCH scheduling enhances
adaptability under dynamic traffic. HRL-TSCH [9] uses hierarchical agents for coordinated slotframe and cell scheduling. RL-SF [25] learns distributed cell allocation from local
states and queues, improving throughput and reducing collisions. QL-TSCH-plus [27] applies Q-learning for per-node

slot/channel adaptation to minimize latency, while ELISE [26]
adjusts slotframe size based on traffic and node density.
Despite improved adaptability, these methods introduce high
computational and energy costs, require training, and face
scalability challenges in dense LLNs.

VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

In this paper, We propose ATSE, an adaptive TSCH scheduler for emergency packets in high-density LLNs. To achieve
precise resource allocation, ATSE adopts subtree-segregated
time-slot allocation with temporal emergency time-slot adjustment, enabling dynamic slot reallocation for emergency
packets that cannot meet real-time constraints and ensuring
low latency. For conflict mitigation, ATSE introduces an
NHash-based mechanism that partitions time-slot segments,
allowing contending packets to access sink resources within
dedicated segments while reducing collision probability and
control overhead. In addition, ATSE incorporates a multi-sink
load balancing mechanism to evenly distribute dynamic traffic
loads across sinks, improving transmission performance and
resource utilization. Implemented on Contiki OS and evaluated
in large-scale high-density scenarios, ATSE outperforms baseline schemes, achieving 18.6% lower latency, 10.5% higher
reliability, and 10.6% lower energy consumption.

For future work, we plan to extend ATSE to multi-hop
LLNs, where end nodes transmit data via multiple intermediate
hops, introducing cumulative latency, higher collision probability, and uneven energy use. We will investigate adaptive
slot allocation considering multi-hop paths and congestion,
enhanced conflict avoidance to prevent cascading collisions,
and potentially predictive or lightweight learning-based approaches to optimize slot assignment under dynamic traffic.
These extensions aim to enable ATSE to support larger, more
complex networks while maintaining low-latency, reliable,
and energy-efficient delivery for both regular and emergency
traffic.
